lesson.title: Personal Economics: Building a Real Budget
lesson.subject: social-studies

contentBlocks.text: This week has studied government structure. Today, this course's other focus: the practical economics of your own future household.

A budget tracks income against expenses over a set period, usually a month. Expenses generally fall into fixed (the same amount each month, like rent) and variable (changes month to month, like food or entertainment) categories. A basic budgeting principle: track every expense category, subtract total expenses from income, and treat what's left as either savings or discretionary spending — never assume there's money left over without actually calculating it. For a monthly income of $2,000 with expenses of $800 (rent), $300 (food), $150 (transportation), and $200 (other): calculate the total expenses, the amount remaining, and what percent of income that remaining amount represents.
You've just built and analyzed a real budget using real arithmetic, not just budgeting in the abstract. Tomorrow we'll review everything from this week.

objectives: Distinguish fixed expenses from variable expenses
Calculate total expenses, remaining income, and savings rate from a real budget scenario
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the shift to personal economics for this lesson.
2. Introduce fixed vs. variable expenses and the basic budgeting principle.
3. Work through the $2,000 income example together, calculating total expenses, remaining amount, and savings rate.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's cumulative review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: work through the calculation one step at a time (sum expenses first, then subtract, then find the percentage) rather than all at once
Ready for more: ask them to identify which of the four expense categories in the example are likely fixed vs. variable, and why
Real, concrete numbers matter here — resist the temptation to skip the actual arithmetic in favor of abstract budgeting talk
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'personal economics' description with a genuine, computed budgeting exercise — the practical skill this half of the course builds toward.
